en: The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Ekottaraja, spoken by the Buddha;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at the Mahāvana Monastery in the city of Vaiśālī.
He was staying at the multi-storied lecture hall together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
all of whom were arhats.
His mind attained mastery and was free from further afflictions;
he exhausted all fetters of existence, possessed the six supernormal powers without obstruction,
and his mind achieved excellent liberation while his wisdom attained excellent liberation.
An elephant king among men,
revered by the gods, humans, and the eight classes of beings;
they were all great arhats and the like.
Furthermore, he was accompanied by a countless multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
who were fully endowed with the immeasurable practices and vows of bodhisattvas and dwelt steadfastly in the dharmas of the merits of all buddhas.
The perfection of wisdom is like the great ocean;
the adornment of merit is like the king of mountains;
with mastery over body and mind, he assumes forms according to the various classes of beings.
To uphold the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means,
they surrounded the World-Honored One, paying respectful homage and making various kinds of offerings;
gazing upon his holy countenance, they praised him with sublime voices.
Desiring only the supreme Dharma of the Tathāgata’s ambrosia—
thus did these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all assemble like clouds.
At that time, the World-Honored One was like a lion king.
Having universally observed the great assembly and understood their thoughts,
he straightened his body, rectified his intention,
and reflected with profound discernment, forming this thought: "My life-force has long since been abandoned."
In reality, there is no phenomenon of birth and death that can undergo transition or extinction.
However, my work is finished and remaining here would be of no benefit;
therefore, in these three months, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
"I should now proclaim this sublime Dharma;
I must not conceal it so that the assembly does not hear it.
Having formed this thought, he immediately addressed the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Follow my words."
All the bhikṣus residing in various worlds were summoned and assembled at this gathering.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana...
Receiving the Honored One’s instruction with the head bowed, he proclaimed, "So be it.
Thereupon, while still in that very seat, he manifested great supernormal powers and ascended into the air.
Like a great elephant king, he reached the summit of Mount Sumeru; having arrived at the mountain peak, he addressed everyone with a great voice:
The sound pervaded a thousandfold world-system.
At that time, forty thousand bhikṣus, having heard his voice,
immediately arrived at this assembly by means of their supernormal powers.
Seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side. At that time,
by the power of great compassion and the power of majestic spiritual authority, the World-Honored One—
He caused the Venerable Śāriputra to conceive a thought.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra had this thought: "Now is precisely the right time."
I shall, by means of the power of my great supernormal knowledges,
go everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm to all bhikṣus—
whether they be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of the Mahāyāna.
Having gathered all together in this great assembly and formed this thought,
they immediately manifested great supernormal powers from these very seats,
pervading the entire trichiliocosm.
All bhikṣus— whether śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those of the Mahāyāna—
assemble in this great gathering;
all these bhikṣus, pratyekabuddhas, and the great assembly of bodhisattvas are hereby addressed.
Having seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:
Namely, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati (Not-Empty-View),
the Youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and the Bodhisattva Cchinnapāpamārgāvaraṇa (Severer of the Obstructions of Evil Paths).
The Bodhisattva Who Severs All Sorrowful Thoughts,
the Bodhisattva Who Thoroughly Penetrates All Practices,
and the Bodhisattva Who Severs All Obstructions.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Gandhahastin Bodhisattva,
and Sthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya and these other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas said: "Good son, follow my words."
Each went to the worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
to all the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—
whether those in their final birth, those who are non-regressive, or those who have attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena.
All have gathered here for this great assembly.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken thus,
the multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—
Each focused their minds to listen to the Buddha’s instructions.
Having heard the instructions, they all rejoiced greatly and cried out, “Excellent, excellent, World-Honored One!”
"It is even so; now is precisely the right time.
Having received these instructions, that assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through their great supernormal powers and by the majestic spiritual authority of the Buddha, [acted accordingly].
Each reached worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions and,
by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, universally announced this to all the bodhisattvas.
Hearing the compassionate summons of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, those bodhisattvas responded.
All of them leaped for joy, unable to contain their delight.
At that time, there were ninety billion hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas,
all of whom were destined to succeed to the position of the Honored One in one more lifetime.
They came to where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas,
all of whom dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there were thirty billion hundred thousand bodhisattvas who had all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Additionally, there were eight billion hundred thousand bodhisattvas.
All of them abide on the stage of practice through faith.
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas arrive one after another in succession;
having seen the Buddha, they prostrate themselves before him with their five limbs touching the ground.
He paid homage to the Blessed One with palms joined in single-minded devotion,
circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, by the power of the Buddha, the Elder Śāriputra—
He clearly perceived and saw that those bodhisattvas, as well as the entire great assembly of this land,
had all gathered at the multi-storied lecture hall in the Great Forest Monastery in the city of Vaiśālī.
With certainty and without doubt, he formed this thought:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
must have long known my mind and its profound contemplation of the sublime meaning."
"I shall ask the Buddha about such a wondrous meaning,
so that all bodhisattvas may eliminate their doubts,
attain unimpeded wisdom, and obtain supreme eloquence."
They shall behold countless Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
they shall hear all the Buddha-dharmas and be able to uphold them entirely,
clearly recollecting them without ever forgetting in the interim.
Up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
I now do so because I desire to cause all bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly to obtain the four kinds of pure dharmas.
What are the four? They are:
the purity of sentient beings and the purity of phenomena.
Because their eloquence is pure;
because the adornments of merit of the Buddha-fields are pure;
and furthermore, because they desire to cause all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly [to attain such purity].
Because one attains the four kinds of mental states that delight in performing subtle and wondrous dharmas.
What are these four? They are as follows:
first, the subtlety of the body.
Because their speech is subtle and wondrous;
because their mind is subtle and wondrous;
and because their skillful means are subtle and wondrous.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dhāraṇīs that enable all bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly to enter [them].
What are these four?
That is to say: the dhāraṇī-door of entering through syllables;
the dhāraṇī-door of skillful mastery in the faculties and conducts of all sentient beings;
and the dhāraṇī-door of skillful mastery in karmic retribution and the practice of non-action.
The Dharma-door of the Profound Endurance of Dharmas and the Dharma-door of the Dhāraṇī;
these twelve subtle and wondrous Dharma-doors are taught so that all bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly may fully attain them.
He formed this thought regarding this subtle and profound meaning:
"I have already mentally examined, articulated, deliberated, and analyzed it;
according to my own intention, I now wish to question the Buddha."
"May the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity for all beings, deign to hear my question.
Having formed this thought, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, will allow me to pose my inquiry."
At that time, out of great compassion, the World-Honored One did not disregard their aspiration and silently granted his consent.
Thereupon, the Elder Śāriputra thought as he had previously.
Thus reflecting in his mind, thus deliberating, and thus discerning,
he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this extensively for the sake of the assembly."
May all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly, by means of this principle, attain purity in all their practices.
Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain this extensively.
At that time, having thus addressed him, the Venerable Śāriputra,
with body and mind established in right mindfulness and his heart moved by a mixture of compassion and joy,
remained silently to one side, gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance.
Their eyes never turned away from him, like those parched with thirst longing for water,
or like hungry bees coveting honey, unable to restrain themselves;
so it was with all those bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly.
At that time, although the World-Honored One knew that the entire great assembly was thirsting with longing,
he spoke to Śāriputra in order to briefly demonstrate the method of practice:
Listen attentively and reflect upon this well;
I shall analyze and explain it to you in detail.
Śāriputra, you should know this.
I now bestow upon you the *dhāraṇī* of the Gate of Entering the Infinite. You,
along with all the bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly—
if you are able, regarding all phenomena...
Without engaging in acceptance or rejection and without granting permission,
one should furthermore be able to firmly uphold each and every phrase— beginning, middle, and end— of this dhāraṇī.
"I shall now analyze and explain this in detail for you,
so that by practicing according to it, you will obtain great benefit and realize it for yourself.
At that time, Śāriputra and the entire assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—
They all raised their voices and said, “Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear and uphold [the teaching] as the World-Honored One has commanded; we are able to practice such conduct.”
“Excellent, World-Honored One! We only pray that you will speak of it.
The Buddha said, “Listen attentively, listen attentively,” and then he spoke the mantra:
*āne māne* (1), *ākhe mākhe* (2), *samanvamukhe* (3), *sajjaye rā*.
1. Mi su mi 2. Si yu ji die (Svayamjitī) 3. Ni lu ji die (Nirjitī) 4. Ni lu ji die (Nirjitī) 5.

Having spoken this "Dhāraṇī of Entering the Boundless Gate," in order to cause all the bodhisattvas and the great assembly to understand the benefits of practice,
he addressed Śāriputra:
You should know this divine mantra:
if any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to practice and study it,
they should understand that all phenomena are not conditioned.
Furthermore, it is neither unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor without perception (*asaṃjñin*), nor without attainment (*anupalambha*).
It is without doubt, without relinquishment, without approval, without arousal, and without movement.
When he contemplates in this manner, [he attains such realization].
With a mind of tranquil extinction, one attains growth and clearly perceives all phenomena as neither created nor uncreated.
It is neither conjoined nor non-conjoined;
it is neither arising nor ceasing;
nor is it past, future, or present.
Nor is there any perception of cessation.
One should neither conceive of "one" nor "two," nor engage in grasping or rejecting.
Without any initial commencement, one should simply practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
When recollecting the Buddha, one does not form a thought of form, nor a thought of non-form;
it is neither with marks nor without marks, neither beautiful nor unbeautiful.
Neither morality nor non-morality;
neither concentration nor non-concentration;
neither wisdom nor non-wisdom.
It is neither liberation nor non-liberation;
neither the knowledge and vision of liberation nor the absence of such knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, it has no birth, no family, and no clan.
It has no retinue; it is neither practice nor non-practice,
neither attainment nor realization.
There are no afflictions, aggregates, elements, or sense bases;
yet, within these afflictions, aggregates, elements, and sense bases, there is also no exhaustion.
It is neither wisdom nor consciousness; it is a non-dharma that cannot be described.
It is not purified by oneself, nor purified by another, nor purified by sentient beings.
It is not for one's own benefit, nor for the benefit of others; it is not the Dharma, nor the Vinaya, nor the purity of practice.
It is not the purity of body, nor the purity of speech, nor the purity of mind.
It is not pure at the prior limit, nor is it pure at the posterior limit;
it is neither self-made nor made by another.
It is in this way, Śāriputra, that one is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
To encompass all dharmas so that they all enter into the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi),
and to know that all dharmas are equal and of one flavor, thereby attaining a mind free from fear—
this is called being a true practitioner of the *dhāraṇī*.
All vows shall be fully satisfied,
for they will resolutely and directly course toward the Bodhi of the Buddha; thus,
no one shall be able to suppress any of their roots of goodness.
By the power of this dhāraṇī, [one attains] the treasury of all dharmas, the various marks and signs of practice,
the spiritual lineage, the provisions, and skillful means.
They will swiftly achieve accomplishment and transcend the sphere of all demonic activities.
Thus it is, Śāriputra.
If a bodhisattva truly attains entry into this boundless gateway of dhāraṇī,
they shall certainly reach the stage of non-retrogression and swiftly arrive at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? It should be known that herein lies the definitive treasury of all Buddhas,
of all dharmas, and of all meritorious qualities.
Furthermore, it can give rise to all the various conceptual activities of sentient beings;
yet, although it definitely gives rise to such merits,
when one exhaustively investigates its essence and characteristics, there is nothing therein that can be apprehended as real.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of all the bodhisattvas and the great assembly:
"Do not harbor doubt regarding the dharma of emptiness; do not conceive of the Buddha as something other."
Furthermore, one who does not waver from the dharma-realm will swiftly obtain dhāraṇīs;
you should listen to such a sūtra as this. Through the dhāraṇī of certainty, they will attain the perfection of wisdom and accomplish the bodhi of the Buddha.
By reciting this dhāraṇī, the bodhisattva is fearless;
all the Buddhas of the ten directions preach the Dharma, which he is able to hear.
That person realizes the principle of the Dharma, equal to the radiance of the sun.
Having attained realization of the unsurpassed Dharma, adorned with the truth of its principles and elegant phrasing,
by reciting and upholding this sutra, one further attains the supreme and sublime dhāraṇī of the subtle essence,
which manifests all things within the gateway of the mind.
In a single eon, all the assemblies each ask about every doubt;
having severed those doubts, their wisdom is inexhaustible.
Such are the Dharma-Princes who draw near to the Bodhi of the Buddha.
Those who receive this entrustment and protect the Dharma, because they love and delight in this sutra,
all sentient beings will cherish them, and all Buddhas will show them compassion;
their fame shall fill the world, for they recite and uphold this mantra.
Furthermore, by virtue of upholding this mantra, when one is on the verge of death,
eight billion Buddhas will extend their hands to receive and support them;
even if one has committed evils over a thousand billion kalpas, one shall still be spared from retribution.
By reciting and upholding this sutra, one becomes pure for an entire month;
even if a bodhisattva diligently practices other merits for ten million eons,
by reciting and upholding this sutra, they will completely surpass them in a single month.
All sentient beings of the three realms, though they may all be demons,
shall be unable to create obstacles because one recites this sutra;
such is the practice of mental application through this supreme dhāraṇī.
They appear universally at that gate; as stated in this sutra, one attains bodhi even until then.
There is no doubt regarding this mantra, for it was spoken by the Omniscient One; therein one attains bodhi.
Because I have heard this dhāraṇī, Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me a prophecy;
I immediately beheld all the Buddhas, their number being like the sands of the Ganges,
and I was able to understand and know all the Dharma they preached.
By diligently reciting this sutra, all shall be swiftly accomplished;
the pure buddha-lands they attain will be adorned with the treasury of radiant marks and the assembly of great śrāvakas, all obtained through this sutra.
If one is not negligent, contemplating with focused attention for seven days upon eighty billion buddhas, they will explain the dhāraṇī:
"That which can be thought should not be thought; do not think, and do not even think of non-thinking."
If one contemplates without conceptualizing and, having contemplated, swiftly attains dharani, it is like reaching the great ocean; do not doubt that there will be no treasures.
If one attains dharani, do not doubt that there will be no reward of bliss.
One who draws near to awakening should apply themselves with vigorous diligence;
if they attain a state of tranquil concentration, they shall likewise attain awakening.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he said:
He spoke again to Śāriputra, saying:
"I now further have four kinds of dhāraṇī-practice methods.
If bodhisattvas are able to fully cultivate and practice within these, [they shall attain success]."
One will certainly attain entry into this gateway dhāraṇī.
What are the four? They are:
abandoning and eliminating covetous desire, and severing the mind of envy.
Toward all sentient beings,
they are able to relinquish everything in giving and feel no regret;
day and night they seek the Dharma, finding joy in the Dharma itself.
Thus it is, Śāriputra.
If a bodhisattva can practice in this manner with full perfection,
they will certainly attain entry into this gateway dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more,
spoke in verse as follows:
"Desire is foul and impure, the domain of Māra, And it is also the causal condition for the hells."
Having realized that sinful karma is the root of the evil realms, he eliminates all envy toward others;
he renounces fame, profit, honor, and close friends. With eyes of love, he gazes levelly upon all sentient beings;
his physical form is upright and most wondrous, and his majestic radiance and virtue are vast, with a composed and graceful countenance.
All conditioned things are the root of contention; One should abandon them and not let them remain.
If one can thus relinquish all craving, One will enter this Dharma-gate.
Diligently seeking all dharmas day and night, With a focused and upright mind, one delights in Bodhi.
"In this way, one can always draw near to the Dharma; the dharani will then fully manifest at the gateway of the mind.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One further addressed Śāriputra:
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that enable one to fulfill all bodhisattva practices and thus attain entry into this gateway dharani.
What are these four?
That is to say, by drawing near to mountain forests and *āraṇya* dwellings, one attains profound *dharmakṣānti*;
one completely renounces fame, profit, offerings, all forms of reverence, and all beloved places.
"Even unto the end of life, he shall never have cause for regret in the interim. Śāriputra,
such a Dharma is able to fully embody all the practices of a bodhisattva."
Having attained this dharani for entering such a gateway,
at that time the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse:
In mountain forests and forest hermitages, which are praised by those of right practice—
though one may dwell in such places— one must be careful not to disparage others;
cultivate patience and heedfulness, always as if one’s head were on fire.
Not relying on fame or profit, He feigns no strange appearances;
Meeting a Buddha is a rare and difficult encounter. Abandoning the home, the source of much suffering, He purifies body, speech, and mind, And reveres the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Seeking neither fame nor profit, knowing contentment in every situation,
like a bird flying through the void with nothing upon which to rely—
such a person as this will never fail to realize the fruit.
One who lacks faith and moral conduct, and does not contemplate the Dharma,
is as far from enlightenment as heaven is from earth;
therefore, a practitioner must renounce fame and profit.
Such is the truly sublime practice, praised by the noble ones.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are four further dharmas that enable one to fully perfect the bodhisattva practice.
One attains entry into such gateways of dhāraṇī.
What are the four? They are the so-called eight kinds of letter-gateways.
If one can skillfully enter into the meaning of these syllables,
one will attain entry into this gateway dhāraṇī. What are the eight?
That is to say: the syllable *pa*, the syllable *ra*,
the syllable *ma*, the syllable *ja*,
the syllable *ka*, and the syllable *ta*.
The syllable *śa* and the syllable *kṣa* together constitute these eight syllables;
*pa* is *tathatā* (suchness).
Because all phenomena enter into selflessness;
because the marks and embellishments of the Tathāgata enter into the non-marks and non-embellishments of the Dharma-body.
"Maṅ" refers to the dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of the noble ones;
they are one and not two, because they enter [into suchness] as one.
"Jra" refers to birth, old age, sickness, and death, which are neither birth, old age, sickness, nor death.
"Ga" refers to entering that which is neither arising nor ceasing.
"Kha" refers to entering that which is both karmic retribution and not karmic retribution.
"Dha" refers to the fact that the dhāraṇī-dharma is fundamentally empty.
Because of entering the dharma-realm that is signless and wishless;
because relinquishment is both concentration and wisdom, and neither concentration nor wisdom,
through entering the single suchness of all dharmas.
*Kṣa* (the conjunct *kṣa*) signifies that all phenomena are empty, inexhaustible, and indestructible,
because they enter into the dharma of primordial quiescence and nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
If one can grasp the meaning of these eight characters,
one will be able to enter this fundamental dharma of the dhāraṇī,
this sūtra of the fundamental dharma of the dhāraṇī.
One should skillfully transcribe, receive, uphold, read, and recite it every half-month or every month.
Furthermore, one should teach this Dharma-text to others, causing them to give rise to joy;
one should encourage their diligent practice and assist in augmenting their spiritual power.
He caused them to focus their minds with diligent effort so as not to regress.
Having spoken thus, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"These four dharmas are able to bring the bodhisattva practice to completion."
Having attained entry into the gateway of dhāraṇī, at that time the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke in verse: "One should contemplate the meaning of the eight syllables, As well as the sūtra and the dhāraṇī."
By copying, upholding, reading, and reciting [this], whether for a month or half a month,
one further transforms other sentient beings; causing them to rejoice and exert themselves,
that person draws near to Bodhi and shall always attain supreme awakening.
Directly beholding all Buddhas dwelling throughout the ten directions, one’s training and practice increase; therefore, one should apply oneself with diligence.
Śāriputra, there are furthermore four other dharmas.
Because it enables one to accomplish all the merits of a bodhisattva,
one should apply oneself with diligence and never retreat within this dhāraṇī.
What are these four?
It is said that all Buddhas of the ten directions shall always protect and mindfully attend to them;
no demonic forces or evil karmas whatsoever shall be able to turn back any of their obstacles of evil karma.
They will swiftly attain purity and unceasing eloquence.
Śāriputra, you should know this:
these four dharmas are able to bring about the fulfillment of the merit of all bodhisattvas.
Within this dhāraṇī, one should apply the mind with single-minded devotion without ever regressing.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

All Buddhas of the ten directions keep [this] in mind; neither Māra nor the works of Māra can prevail, for they are able to transform karmic obstructions and render them pure, swiftly attaining supreme and excellent eloquence.
Śāriputra, I recall that in a past life...
For vast, immeasurable, and boundless asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
exceeding even that number,

there was at that time a Buddha named Ratnaguṇatejośvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, as that Buddha was about to enter nirvana, he extensively preached this *dhāraṇī* of the Root of Dharma for the great assembly.
At that moment, there was a great wheel-turning king named Dhṛtapradīpa.
Endowed with the seven treasures, the people lived in peace and happiness.
At that time, the king had a son named Acintyaguṇavikrama,
who, at the age of sixteen, [went] to that Tathāgata.
Having heard this Dharani-dharmaparyaya, they rejoiced and,
for seventy thousand years, [practiced it].
Diligently practice this dhāraṇī-dharma-text;
do not sleep nor recline, but remain seated upright in one place;
do not covet wealth or property, do not crave royal rank, and take no pleasure in your own person.
He encountered ninety billion hundred thousand nayutas of Buddhas.
He was able to hear all the teachings these Buddhas preached, and having heard them, he was able to retain them.
He took joy in practicing them and grew weary of the ways of household life.
Having shaved off his hair and beard to become a śramaṇa,
he further practiced this "Dhāraṇī of the Entrance into the Gate of the Infinite" for ninety thousand years until it was fully perfected.
Having brought them to full maturity, he further uses these verses to analyze and reveal the truth extensively for the sake of sentient beings,
exerting his strength and diligence in teaching and transforming them throughout his entire life.
He caused eight hundred billion nayutas of sentient beings to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; from that moment of generating the resolve,
they accumulated merit and cultivated virtue.
All have established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression. Śāriputra, you should know this:
at that time, there was an elder named Candravyūha.
He had a son named Anantaprabha, who,
having heard from that bhikṣu this *dhāraṇī* of the Dharma-source for entering the gate of the infinite,
gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of these roots of goodness resulting from this sympathetic joy,
one shall encounter ninety billion Buddhas and attain the supreme dhāraṇī.
They attain the Dharma-gate of generating supreme faith,
such that all who hear their speech will respectfully follow it;
furthermore, they attain supreme, uninterrupted eloquence.
Surpassing all the assemblies of bodhisattvas,
he constantly made offerings to all those Tathāgatas throughout three kalpas.
Having completed those three kalpas, he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra, you should know now:
do not give rise to doubt or harbor thoughts of obstruction.
At that time, was the son of a householder named Candraketu anyone else? [It was none other than myself.]
That was none other than the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara.
And as for the bhikṣu Acintyaguṇaviśeṣa who preached the Dharma at that time, could he have been anyone else?
He was none other than the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha.
Śāriputra, I and all the bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa,
upon hearing this fundamental dharma, have all given rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
Because I, at that time, gave rise to a superior mind of sympathetic joy, [I have attained this].
By virtue of these roots of goodness,
all afflictions throughout four million kalpas are completely transcended and can no longer act as obstacles.
In the presence of nine billion buddhas, he heard the True Dharma,
attained the supreme dhāraṇī,
and further acquired the supreme dharma-gate of giving rise to faith.
Furthermore, they shall attain the supreme, continuous, and uninterrupted eloquence.
Śāriputra, you should know this:
if any bodhisattvas wish to swiftly reach unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, [they should cultivate this].
Even if one is unable to practice fully, one should hear this dhāraṇī and give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy. Why is this?
Because by means of the roots of goodness resulting from hearing and rejoicing, [one will attain liberation].
It can serve as a superior cause for the stage of non-retrogression,
and even until one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
it likewise serves as a superior causal condition by virtue of these roots of goodness.
How much more so for those who copy, read, recite, receive, and uphold it;
who practice according to the Dharma and explain it extensively for others;
and who praise and encourage others to study and practice it.
This accumulation of merits can be known only by the Buddhas;
no sentient being is able to describe it in its entirety.
As for what can be known through calculation and deliberation:
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words,
wishing to reiterate this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"Hearing the sutra and rejoicing in one's heart, Transcribing it, as well as reading and reciting it."
Holding it oneself and teaching others to hold it—
this mass of all merits cannot be measured by any sentient beings;
having directly beheld all Buddhas, one attains rare and marvelous faith.
Capable of knowing all, they swiftly realize sublime enlightenment through the most profound sūtras;
they behold the Buddhas without fail and attain meditative concentration,
supernormal powers, exquisite form, and the provisions for awakening.
The dhāraṇīs and so forth are without decrease; I recall that in past lives, up until supreme enlightenment, I heard such boundless dhāraṇīs as these,
And thereby beheld Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
May they realize according to their inclinations;
When the Honored One Dīpaṃkara was accomplishing [enlightenment] in his boundless previous lives,
I and the assembly of this Bhadrakalpa all rejoiced together as Amitābha preached the Dharma for us.
Those who wish to swiftly realize enlightenment, Subdue all māras,
and be endowed with the marks of a hundred merits— For them, practicing this dharma is not difficult.
The merit of writing, upholding, and reciting it Is that of a true son of the Buddha.
Even if all worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
were filled with jewels and offered to the Muni,
the merit of one who upholds this [sūtra] by means of writing it down would surpass that [offering].
By the power of this sutra, it will not be difficult for one to necessarily attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva enters into this boundless dhāraṇī...
As for those who apply themselves with diligent effort,
eight yakṣas within that Snowy Mountain will constantly come day and night to protect such a person.
By means of their majestic power, they enter all the pores of that person's body.
What are these eight?
Their names are the Yakṣa Vīryavanta (Valiant) and the Yakṣa Dṛḍha (Firm).
The yakṣa Bahubala, the yakṣa Nārāyaṇabala, the yakṣa Satyavratī, the yakṣa Anabhibhūta,
the yakṣa Dīrghadaṃṣṭrotkaṭa, and the yakṣa Subhuja.
Śāriputra, in this manner,
if these bodhisattvas wish to cause those eight great yakṣas to appear before them in bodily form,
they should bathe themselves clean, put on fine, pure garments, and enter the path of practice or the maṇḍala.
If one does not give rise to evil thoughts toward any sentient being and single-mindedly recollects this dhāraṇī, the root of all dharmas,
those eight yakṣas will swiftly appear before one’s face.
May this bodhisattva clearly behold them.
Furthermore, there are eight bodhisattvas born among the devas of the desire realm who also constantly protect and mind those who practice this dhāraṇī.
What are these eight?
Their names are as follows: namely, the Devaputra Vimala-prabhāsa, the Devaputra Samanta-prabhāsa, the Devaputra Jñāna-prabha, and the Devaputra Sūrya-prabha.
The Devaputra Adhyeṣaka, the Devaputra Sarvāśāparipūraka,
the Devaputra Nakṣatrarāja, and the Devaputra Ratnamati—
these eight devaputras shall always protect and keep [this] in mind.
If one practices this dhāraṇī, one must necessarily apply oneself with a refined mind and focused attention in this manner.
A bodhisattva should give rise to a vow of truthfulness.
Recognizing kindness and repaying it, they seek the Dharma day and night;
finding delight in the Dharma, they cultivate the profound patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Such a bodhisattva must practice giving and distribute it among others.
One should give to others according to what one possesses;
even if one has only this single item, it must be given to others.
In this way, the bodhisattva must further show reverence to all, with a humble mind and submissive conduct.
With single-minded focus, they should study the profound patience.
All bodhisattvas should practice the dhāraṇī-dharma-mūla in this manner.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was expounding this Dharma-text of the dhāraṇī,
there were among the assembly thirty billion hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
All of them attained the stage of non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There was an assembly of sixty billion hundred thousand nayutas of devas and humans.
Those who had not yet resolved their minds [for enlightenment] all attained the resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"What should this sutra be named?
How should we, the great assembly, uphold it?
The Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra, saying:
This sutra is titled "The Dhāraṇī of Entering the Source of Boundless Dharmas.
To receive and uphold this sutra in this manner is also called "the Solemnly Arising Bodhisattva."
One should uphold this sutra in this way;
it is also called "Subduing All Māras and Enemies," and one should uphold it in this way because it is called "Definitively Proceeding Toward All-Knowledge. One should uphold it thus.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra,
the Venerable Śāriputra, the śrāvakas, the great assembly of bodhisattvas,
and the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, [rejoiced].
The entire assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Ekāntika-udgata Spoken by the Buddha.
